newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition says unrest could turn violent.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition says unrest could turn violent.

text.p: An opposition leader warned on Thursday that Serbia's wave of unrest might turn violent under police pressure, as thousands of protesters took to the streets for the 46th consecutive day.

The influential Serbian Orthodox Church, long a pillar of autocratic government, broke six weeks of silence by condemning the ruling Socialists (SPS) for election fraud which triggered the mass demonstrations.

Daily protests by up to a quarter of a million people have called on President Slobodan Milosevic to reverse the Socialists' annulment of victories by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition in local polls on November 17.

Protests were peaceful until a December 24 riot between Zajedno activists and government loyalists bused into Belgrade from the provinces. Street marches were promptly banned and police have sporadically assaulted protesters since then.
Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, claimed in a Reuters Television interview that Milosevic was plotting bloody repression with the help of shadowy militia gangs.

"Milosevic is in the process of forming an alliance with (Serbian) paramilitary groups previously involved in the war in Bosnia and Croatia to set up terrorist attacks against the opposition," he said.

Draskovic said Zajedno's principle of non-violence remained intact but, if police attacks worsened, "nobody can give guarantees people would not reply in a way of self-defence to protect their lives and human dignity.
"Unfortunately this could be the beginning of bloodshed and civil war," said Draskovic, who in 1992 was badly beaten during a spell in police detention.
"I have no wish to topple Milosevic in the street. I want to defeat him in democratic elections," he added.
Zajedno sprang into the international spotlight after being stripped of victory in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns, including the capital Belgrade.
About 250,000 Zajedno faithful welcomed the New Year in Belgrade with a city-centre rally featuring ringing alarm clocks as a shrill warning to President Slobodan Milosevic that his "time is up".

He had just delivered a New Year's message on state television saying 1996 had been a very good year, making no mention of the most sustained challenge to leftist rule in Serbian-led Yugoslavia for 50 years.

About 25,000 protesters assembled in central Belgrade on Thursday but were blocked by riot police when they tried to sweep out of a pedestrian mall towards a major street. They dispersed later. No clashes were reported.

In a statement faxed to Reuters, the Holy Synod of the Serbian Orthodox Church said that during an extraordinary session on Thursday it had "strongly condemned the regime which has flagrantly trampled on the will of the people.
"The... church strongly condemns the forging of people's votes, stifling of political and religious freedoms and especially the beating up and murder of people on the streets."
One Zajedno demonstrator was reportedly trampled to death on December 24, while another was shot and critically wounded by a government supporter.

Western governments have told Milosevic that Yugoslavia can forget about reconstruction aid for an economy prostrated by U.N. sanctions and SPS corruption unless he restores Zajedno's election victories and starts broader democratic reform.
Milosevic pledged significant privatisation in 1997 but said nothing about political liberalisation, which would entail opposition access to the SPS-dominated mainstream media.
State television aired footage of New Year street celebrations in many cities abroad but ignored the huge outdoor festival organised by Zajedno in Belgrade.

"This (New Year), Belgrade was the capital of Planet Earth for everyone except the president of this state and his television," Zoran Djindjic, one of Zajedno's leaders, told Thursday's throng in Republic Square.

"We want to go forward, we want to become part of Europe -- but our dictator cannot comprehend that," said Vesna Pesic, another protest leader. "How does he propose to launch reforms when he is closing the door to the world?"
